content.text: Reading a value, changing it in code and writing it back isn't safe just because it runs inside a transaction. At the default
level, two requests can read the same value, and the second write silently replaces the first. Let the database do the arithmetic in one
, check a version when you write, or lock the row when you read it.

An inventory count finds 5 desk lamps on the shelf, but the product page says 8 are in stock. Two orders, for 3 lamps and 2, arrived a second apart, and the reservation code did what most code does: load the product, subtract the quantity in C#, save, all inside a transaction. In a test on SQL Server 2022 with two sessions, session A read a stock of 10, session B read 10 a second later, A wrote 7 and committed, then B wrote 8 and committed. Both updates reported 1 row affected, nothing failed, and the shop now promises 3 lamps it doesn't have. The same test on PostgreSQL 18 also ended at 8.
The belief: reading a value, changing it in application code and writing it back is safe as long as all three steps run inside one transaction.

It's a reasonable belief. Transactions are taught as the tool for concurrency, and "isolation" sounds like nobody else can touch the rows you're working on. ORMs make the pattern the default: load an entity, change a property, call

. And on a laptop with one user, nobody else writes between your read and your write. The isolation levels article earlier in this path covered what the default level lets reads see; this one covers writes.

Microsoft's locking guide describes it exactly: lost updates occur when two or more transactions select the same row and then update it based on the value originally selected, and the last update overwrites the others. At
, SQL Server releases a shared lock as soon as the read completes, so nothing stops a second transaction from reading the same 10 a moment later. Then comes the write. EF Core sends
, a constant your process computed. The database can't know that 7 came from a value that's no longer current, so it writes it, and the next writer replaces it. That's a
, and the transaction around it doesn't prevent it.
Fix 1: let the database do the arithmetic
UPDATE Products SET Stock = Stock - @qty WHERE Id = @id AND Stock >= @qty

reads and writes in one statement. A second update of the same row waits until the first transaction ends. PostgreSQL's docs describe what happens next at Read Committed: the waiting updater re-evaluates its
clause against the updated version of the row and applies its change to that version. In the test, session B waited about a second for A's commit, then took the stock from 7 to 5. The guard in
: when there isn't enough stock, the update matches 0 rows instead of going negative.
Fix 2: check a version when you write
Not every change fits in one
: someone editing a product page reads the row, thinks for a minute and saves the whole form. Keep the read, but make the write conditional: add a
column, which SQL Server changes on every update, and update only
: no locks, and the late writer finds out. In the T-SQL test, B's update matched 0 rows. EF Core adds that condition for you when the property is marked
. In a test with EF Core 10, the second
: "The database operation was expected to affect 1 row(s), but actually affected 0 row(s)".
Fix 3: lock the row when you read it
When the logic between the read and the write is too complex for SQL but runs in one short transaction, take the lock at read time. SQL Server's
hint takes update locks and holds them until the transaction completes, and only one transaction can hold an update lock on a row. PostgreSQL's
locks the rows as though for update, blocking other updates, deletes and
reads until the transaction ends. In both tests, B's locked read waited for A's commit, returned 7, and the stock ended at 5.
A stricter level turns the bug into an error
keeps shared locks to the end of the transaction. In the test, both sessions held one, each
waited for the other's lock, and SQL Server picked B as the deadlock victim with Msg 1205. Microsoft's guide describes this select-then-update deadlock and recommends
to avoid it. PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read doesn't lock reads: in the test, B's update failed with
could not serialize access due to concurrent update
. Nothing was lost, but one order failed, and it only succeeds if your code retries the whole transaction.

content.text: When the new value can't be computed in SQL, use one of the other two patterns:

blocks.code:
-- Optimistic (SQL Server): write only if the row is unchanged
UPDATE dbo.Products SET Stock = @newStock
WHERE Id = @id AND Version = @versionRead; -- test: B got 0 rows

-- Pessimistic (SQL Server): hold an update lock until COMMIT
SELECT Stock FROM dbo.Products WITH (UPDLOCK) WHERE Id = @id;

-- Pessimistic (PostgreSQL)
SELECT stock FROM products WHERE id = $1 FOR UPDATE;

blocks.title: A retry must start from the read

content.text: When a version check fails, or a transaction is rolled back after Msg 1205 or a serialization error, rerun everything from the read: load the current row, repeat the check, compute the new value. EF Core's docs show refreshing the original values so the next save passes the check; doing that without recomputing writes the stale decision again.
